title-group.article-title: Impact of Intraprostatic Simultaneous Integrated Boost on Long‐Term Outcomes in Unfavorable Intermediate‐Risk Prostate Cancer Treated With Dose‐Escalated Radiotherapy and Short‐Term Androgen Deprivation Therapy

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Unfavorable intermediate‐risk prostate cancer (UIR‐PCa) represents a biologically heterogeneous subgroup with a higher risk of recurrence compared with favorable intermediate‐risk disease. Contemporary management frequently includes dose‐escalated radiotherapy (RT) combined with short‐term androgen deprivation therapy (ADT). Whether additional intraprostatic dose escalation using a simultaneous integrated boost (SIB) provides incremental oncologic benefit in this setting remains uncertain.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We retrospectively analyzed 194 patients with UIR‐PCa treated at three institutions between 2010 and 2023. All patients received image‐guided intensity‐modulated or volumetric modulated arc RT to 78 Gy with short‐term ADT. An MRI‐guided intraprostatic SIB (up to 86 Gy) was delivered in 77 patients (39.7%) at clinician discretion. Primary endpoints were biochemical recurrence‐free survival (bRFS), distant metastasis‐free survival (DMFS), and prostate cancer–specific mortality (PCSM). Multivariable Cox and competing‐risk regression models were used to assess predictors of outcome.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: After a median follow‐up of 105 months, 8‐year bRFS and DMFS rates for the entire cohort were 93.7% and 95.7%, respectively. Addition of SIB was not associated with improved bRFS (93.5% vs 93.6%, p = 0.36), DMFS (94.6% vs 96.7%, p = 0.15), or PCSM. Percent positive biopsy cores ≥ 50% was the only independent predictor of inferior bRFS on multivariable analysis. Treatment‐related toxicity was low in both groups, with no significant differences in late grade ≥ 2 gastrointestinal or genitourinary toxicity.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In patients with UIR‐PCa uniformly treated with dose‐escalated, image‐guided RT and short‐term ADT, long‐term oncologic outcomes were excellent. The addition of an intraprostatic SIB was safe but did not confer measurable improvement in biochemical or distant disease control. These findings support a selective rather than routine use of focal intraprostatic dose escalation in contemporary UIR‐PCa management.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Radiotherapy (RT), with or without androgen‐deprivation therapy (ADT), is a cornerstone of curative treatment for intermediate‐risk prostate cancer (IR‐PCa). However, IR‐PCa encompasses biologically heterogeneous tumors with variable risks of recurrence and metastasis. Contemporary guidelines, including those of the NCCN, subdivide IR‐PCa into favorable (FIR) and unfavorable (UIR) subgroups on the basis of multiple risk factors, higher Gleason patterns, and a greater proportion of positive biopsy cores [1, 2, 3]. UIR disease is associated with greater tumor burden and a metastatic profile approaching that of high‐risk patients, and thus often warrants treatment intensification [4, 5].

Randomized trials such as RTOG 9408 and TROG 96.01 established that short‐term ADT (4–6 months) combined with RT improves biochemical and disease‐specific outcomes in IR‐PCa [6, 7]. Subsequent dose‐escalation studies, including RTOG 0126, MRC RT01, and the Dutch multicenter trial, demonstrated that RT doses ≥ 74 Gy improve local control versus conventional regimens, leading to widespread adoption of high‐dose, image‐guided techniques as the contemporary standard [8, 9, 10]. In this setting, many UIR patients already receive dose‐escalated RT plus short‐term ADT as routine care.

The simultaneous integrated boost (SIB) was developed to selectively escalate dose to intraprostatic lesions (IPLs) while maintaining organ‐at‐risk constraints and overall treatment time [11, 12]. The phase III FLAME trial reported improved biochemical disease‐free survival with MRI‐guided intraprostatic boosting to 95 Gy, without significant gains in metastasis‐free or overall survival [13]. Most FLAME participants had intermediate‐ or high‐risk disease and were treated before the routine integration of multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) and prostate‐specific membrane antigen PET/CT (PSMA‐PET/CT), which now allow more precise lesion localization and staging.

Retrospective series, including multi‐institutional and propensity‐matched analyses, suggest that SIB can further enhance local control with acceptable toxicity [14, 15, 16]. However, the incremental value of SIB in UIR patients who already receive guideline‐concordant short‐term ADT and uniform dose‐escalated, image‐guided RT remains unclear. In a population where distant relapse and occult micrometastatic disease may dominate long‐term outcomes, additional intraprostatic dose intensification may yield diminishing returns.

We therefore conducted a multi‐institutional retrospective analysis to evaluate whether SIB confers additional biochemical or distant control in patients with UIR‐PCa treated uniformly with dose‐escalated RT and short‐term ADT. Our primary objective was to determine whether focal boosting provides meaningful clinical or prognostic benefit beyond contemporary standard‐dose regimens in this biologically unfavorable subgroup.

sec.title: Patient Selection
sec.p: This retrospective multi‐institutional study (Başkent University IRB No. KA13/146) included patients with UIR‐PCa treated with definitive RT and short‐term ADT across three tertiary centers between 2010 and 2023. A total of 356 patients were screened; 150 who did not receive ADT and 12 who received ADT > 12 months were excluded, leaving 194 eligible patients.

All patients met NCCN criteria for UIR disease, defined by the presence of ≥ 2 intermediate‐risk factors or Gleason Grade Group 3. To ensure treatment uniformity, only patients who received 6–12 months of ADT and had a minimum follow‐up of 24 months were included. Patients with high‐risk features, prior pelvic RT, metastatic disease, prolonged ADT (> 12 months), or incomplete clinical data were excluded.

Staging included digital rectal examination, PSA assessment, mpMRI when available, and bone scintigraphy. PSMA‐PET/CT was performed selectively in more recent years. Of the entire cohort, 29.9% underwent PSMA‐PET/CT, 67.5% mpMRI, and 12.4% conventional CT and bone scan.

sec.title: Imaging and Target Delineation
sec.p: Treatment‐planning CT scans were obtained at 3‐mm slice thickness. When available, mpMRI (T2‐weighted, diffusion‐weighted, and dynamic contrast–enhanced sequences) was rigidly fused to the planning CT. The IPL was defined by the treating radiation oncologist and a genitourinary radiologist.

The clinical target volume (CTV) included the prostate and proximal seminal vesicles. Planning target volume (PTV) expansions were 7–8 mm, reduced posteriorly to 5 mm [11, 17]. Organs at risk included bladder, rectum, bowel, and femoral heads.

sec.title: Treatment Characteristics
sec.p: All patients received definitive IMRT or VMAT to a total dose of 78 Gy in 39 fractions. Daily cone‐beam CT ensured accurate setup. A SIB of up to 86 Gy was delivered to the IPL at clinician discretion when MRI clearly identified a lesion and organ‐at‐risk constraints could be met. SIB was withheld when MRI was inadequate for lesion definition or when anatomic limitations precluded safe escalation.

All patients received short‐term ADT with an LHRH agonist or antagonist, initiated 2–3 months before or concurrently with RT, for a median duration of 6 months. ADT duration did not differ between SIB and non‐SIB cohorts.

sec.title: Follow‐up and Endpoints
sec.p: Patients were evaluated every 3–6 months for 5 years and annually thereafter. BR was defined using the Phoenix criterion (nadir PSA + 2 ng/mL). LR was defined as intraprostatic or regional nodal failure; distant metastasis included nonregional nodal or visceral spread.
Primary endpoints were bRFS, DMFS, and PCSM. Toxicities were prospectively graded per RTOG/EORTC criteria; late toxicity was defined as events occurring ≥ 90 days after RT.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Analyses were performed using SPSS v25.0 and R v4.3.3 (packages: survival, cmprsk, timeROC, riskRegression, rmda). Baseline characteristics were compared using chi‐square or Wilcoxon tests. Standardized mean differences (SMDs) quantified clinical balance independent of sample size. Kaplan–Meier curves and log‐rank tests evaluated bRFS and DMFS. Competing‐risk analyses using cumulative incidence functions and Gray's test assessed PCSM, treating non–cancer mortality as a competing event. Univariable and multivariable Cox models identified predictors of bRFS and DMFS; variables with p < 0.10 in univariable analyses were entered into multivariable models. Fine–Gray regression evaluated predictors of PCSM.

To assess incremental prognostic value of SIB, two nested multivariable models were compared: 1.

Base + SIB Model.

Model performance was evaluated using Akaike and Bayesian information criteria (AIC, BIC), time‐dependent ROC curves (60 and 96 months), Brier scores, decile‐based calibration plots, decision‐curve analysis, and ω‐statistics. Statistical significance was set at two‐sided p < 0.05.

sec.title: Patient and Treatment Characteristics
sec.p: A total of 194 UIR‐PCa patients were included, of whom 77 (39.7%) received SIB. Median age was 70 years (IQR, 65–75), and median PSA was 11.3 ng/mL (IQR, 7.6–15.6). Baseline demographic, clinical, and treatment variables were well balanced between groups (all standardized mean differences < 0.25) (Table 1). All patients received dose‐escalated RT (78 Gy) with short‐term ADT for a median of 6 months, with no difference between SIB and non‐SIB cohorts (p = 0.51).

sec.title: Treatment Outcomes
sec.p: After a median follow‐up of 105.5 months (IQR, 80.4–130.6), the 8‐year bRFS and DMFS rates for the entire cohort were 93.7% and 95.7%, respectively. At last follow‐up, 152 patients (78.3%) were alive; 5 deaths (2.6%) were attributed to PCa.

SIB did not improve bRFS (93.5% vs 93.6%; p = 0.36) or DMFS (94.6% vs 96.7%; p = 0.15) (Figure 1). In univariable analysis, percent positive biopsy cores and ADT duration were associated with bRFS, whereas no clinical variable significantly predicted DMFS (Table 2). On multivariable modeling, percent positive cores ≥ 50% remained the only independent predictor of inferior bRFS (HR = 5.92; 95% CI, 1.65–10.11; p = 0.02). Younger age (< 70 years) demonstrated borderline significance (p = 0.05).

sec.p: A total of five PCSM events (2.6%) occurred. In competing‐risk analysis, neither SIB nor ADT duration was associated with PCSM (p = 0.62 and p = 0.73, respectively). Although unadjusted Gray's test showed a marginally lower cumulative incidence of PCSM in the SIB group (p = 0.04), this signal did not persist in multivariable Fine–Gray models, reflecting the very low event number.

sec.title: Prognostic Model Performance
sec.p: The base multivariable model demonstrated good discrimination for biochemical relapse‐free survival, with a 96‐month AUC of 0.74 (95% CI, 0.69–0.79). Inclusion of SIB did not improve discrimination at either 60 or 96 months and was not associated with a reduction in prediction error. Model parsimony worsened with the addition of SIB, as reflected by higher Akaike and Bayesian information criteria (Table 3).

sec.p: Consistent with these findings, ω‐statistics demonstrated a negligible contribution of SIB to overall prognostic information (range, 0.0%–0.3%). Decision‐curve analysis showed nearly identical net clinical benefit between models with and without SIB across clinically relevant threshold probabilities (0.05–0.30), indicating no added value of SIB for risk‐based decision‐making (Figure 2A,B).

sec.p: Calibration at 96 months was acceptable for both models, with good agreement between predicted and observed event rates. Mild overestimation was observed in the highest risk deciles, but inclusion of SIB did not materially improve calibration performance (Figure 2C,D).

sec.title: Toxicity Outcomes
sec.p: Acute and late toxicities were low across the cohort. Most patients experienced no GI toxicity (77.8%) or no GU toxicity (49.4%). Late grade ≥ 2 events were uncommon: 7.6% GI and 15.4% GU, with only one grade 3 GU event. SIB was not associated with increased grade ≥ 2 GI (p = 0.25) or GU toxicity (p = 0.79).
At 8 years, cumulative incidence of grade ≥ 2 GI toxicity was comparable between SIB and non‐SIB (7.2% vs 7.1%; p = 0.89). Grade ≥ 2 GU toxicity was also similar (12.4% vs 9.5%; p = 0.87) (Figure 3).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this multi‐institutional cohort of patients with UIR‐PCa treated with contemporary image‐guided RT, uniform whole‐gland dose escalation, and short‐term ADT, the addition of an intraprostatic SIB did not improve biochemical or distant disease control. Long‐term outcomes were excellent across both groups, reflecting the effectiveness of optimized combined‐modality therapy in this risk category. Importantly, SIB also failed to improve discrimination, calibration, or clinical utility across multiple model‐performance metrics, indicating no incremental prognostic value beyond established clinical factors.

Prospective data help contextualize these observations. The phase III FLAME trial demonstrated that MRI‐guided boosting improved biochemical disease‐free survival but did not translate into metastasis‐free or overall survival advantages at long‐term follow‐up [13, 18]. Likewise, early analyses from PIVOTALboost and institutional series show high local control with focal or whole‐gland escalation, yet consistent failure to demonstrate meaningful improvement in systemic outcomes [19]. Systematic reviews consistently show excellent biochemical outcomes after focal boosting, typically 92%–98% at 5 years, yet fail to identify meaningfully improved long‐term systemic control [20, 21], These findings imply that the incremental benefits of local intensification diminish when background control rates are already high, and when long‐term prognosis is driven predominantly by non‐local progression.

Importantly, our findings should be interpreted as complementary to—not contradictory of—prior focal boost trials, particularly the FLAME study. FLAME demonstrated that MRI‐guided intraprostatic boosting can improve biochemical disease‐free survival, establishing the safety and feasibility of focal dose escalation [13, 18]. However, despite improved biochemical control, FLAME did not demonstrate gains in metastasis‐free or overall survival with long‐term follow‐up, underscoring that enhanced local control does not necessarily translate into improved systemic outcomes when background treatment is already effective.

In contrast to FLAME, the present study specifically focused on a contemporary cohort of patients with UIR‐PCa uniformly treated with whole‐gland dose‐escalated RT, daily image guidance, and short‐term ADT, reflecting current guideline‐concordant practice [1]. Within this optimized treatment context, baseline biochemical and distant control rates were already excellent, approaching a ceiling effect. Under such conditions, the opportunity for additional intraprostatic dose intensification to meaningfully alter long‐term oncologic outcomes appears limited.

Biological considerations further support this interpretation. Although UIR disease is categorized as localized, it carries a higher probability of occult extraprostatic extension or micrometastatic spread than FIR disease. Several retrospective and meta‐analytic studies demonstrate that distant progression, not isolated LR, is the primary determinant of long‐term outcomes in aggressive localized PCa [22]. When whole‐gland EQD2 doses exceed ~80 Gy, local control approaches a ceiling effect [23, 24], and the radiosensitizing effect of ADT further reduces the likelihood that persistent intraprostatic disease is the dominant mechanism of failure. Under these conditions, additional focal dose escalation is unlikely to meaningfully alter the natural history of UIR disease.

Taken together, our findings support a selective rather than routine role for intraprostatic boosting in UIR‐PCa. When whole‐gland dose escalation and systemic therapy are appropriately delivered, treatment outcomes appear to be driven predominantly by underlying tumor biology rather than residual intraprostatic disease. In this setting, additional focal escalation should be individualized and guided by clearly defined biological or imaging risk features, rather than applied universally.

Advanced staging may also influence the measurable impact of SIB. PSMA‐PET/CT provides substantially improved sensitivity and specificity for detecting nodal and DM compared with conventional imaging, as demonstrated in proPSMA and subsequent multicenter trials [25, 26, 27, 28]. Upstaging rates of 10%–20% have been reported even within intermediate‐risk populations. In the present cohort, only ~30% of patients underwent PSMA‐PET/CT, reflecting its recent clinical adoption. Under‐staging due to limited use of PSMA‐PET/CT may have diluted any observable benefit from intraprostatic boosting, as outcomes among occult node‐positive or micrometastatic patients would be determined by systemic rather than local disease burden.

Beyond SIB, our study identified percent positive biopsy cores as the only independent predictor of bRFS. This aligns with prior reports demonstrating its role as an indicator of intraprostatic tumor burden, multifocality, or aggressive histology [2, 29, 30]. Percent positive cores appears to capture biologic risk more accurately than PSA, T stage, or ISUP grade in UIR populations, and its persistent significance despite adjustment for SIB highlights the dominant influence of underlying tumor burden on recurrence risk. Although longer ADT duration showed a univariable association with improved bRFS, this effect disappeared in multivariable analysis, likely reflecting confounding by indication; patients with higher‐risk features tended to receive slightly longer ADT. Randomized trials indicate that most benefit for IR‐PCa is achieved with 4–6 months of ADT [31, 32, 33], consistent with our findings.

SIB was delivered safely, with low rates of grade ≥ 2 GI and GU toxicity, consistent with prior boost and dose‐escalation trials [13, 18, 34]. The use of VMAT, MRI fusion, daily IGRT, and strict adherence to dose constraints likely contributed to the favorable toxicity profile [35]. Collectively, these results support the feasibility of focal boosting but do not demonstrate a clear clinical rationale for its routine use in patients already receiving optimized whole‐gland dose‐escalated RT and ADT.

Looking forward, advances in biologically guided targeting may better identify patients who could benefit from intensified local therapy. PSMA‐PET/CT, high‐resolution mpMRI, and radiomic signatures offer opportunities to delineate IPLs more accurately and differentiate biologically aggressive subvolumes [36, 37, 38, 39, 40]. Ongoing trials, including PIVOTALboost (NCT04186845), BOOSTER (NCT05539368), FLAME‐2, and HypoFocal‐SBRT (NCT04835558), are evaluating PSMA‐ or MRI‐defined dose painting approaches that may improve outcomes beyond those achievable with uniform whole‐gland escalation. Integration of imaging biomarkers with molecular and genomic classifiers may further refine patient selection for focal dose intensification and help define subgroups where SIB provides clinically meaningful benefit.

This study has limitations inherent to its retrospective, non‐randomized design, including potential selection bias related to MRI availability and institutional practice patterns. The small number of PCSM events limits statistical power for detecting between‐group differences. PSMA‐PET/CT was available in only a subset of patients, reflecting the evolving imaging landscape over the study period. As a result, some cases may have been under‐staged using conventional imaging; however, this limitation is inherent to the historical availability of advanced staging modalities and does not alter the internal validity of the comparative SIB analysis. Finally, physician‐reported toxicity scoring may undercapture lower‐grade or patient‐perceived symptoms.

Despite these limitations, the study has several notable strengths. It includes one of the largest UIR‐specific cohorts treated with uniform high‐dose IGRT and standardized short‐term ADT, providing a rigorous assessment of whether focal boosting has incremental value in this well‐defined population. The long follow‐up (> 8 years), homogeneous treatment protocols, and comprehensive competing‐risk and multimetric model evaluation enhance the robustness and generalizability of our findings.

From a multidisciplinary and urology‐focused perspective, these findings have important implications for shared decision‐making in patients with UIR‐PCa. In the setting of contemporary dose‐escalated, image‐guided RT combined with short‐term ADT, long‐term biochemical and distant disease control rates appear to be already optimized, limiting the potential incremental benefit of routine intraprostatic dose escalation. Under these conditions, treatment outcomes are likely driven more by underlying tumor biology than by residual intraprostatic disease. Consistent with this interpretation, percent positive biopsy cores emerged as the only independent predictor of biochemical failure, underscoring tumor burden as a more relevant determinant of outcome than focal dose intensification. Together, these results support a selective, individualized approach to intraprostatic boosting, in which patient‐specific risk features and tumor burden are prioritized over routine escalation, and reinforce the value of multidisciplinary discussion when tailoring treatment strategies for UIR‐PCa.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this multi‐institutional cohort of patients with UIR‐PCa treated with uniform dose‐escalated, image‐guided RT and standardized short‐term ADT, the addition of a SIB to the IPL was safe but provided no improvement in biochemical control, DMFS, PCSM, or prognostic model performance. These findings suggest that routine intraprostatic boosting offers limited added value when whole‐gland dose escalation and systemic therapy are already optimized. Limited PSMA‐PET/CT staging in this cohort may have contributed to under‐staging and attenuated the measurable impact of focal dose escalation. Future research incorporating comprehensive PSMA‐PET/CT, biologically informed imaging, radiomics, and molecular profiling is needed to identify subgroups that may meaningfully benefit from targeted focal intensification.
